title: BBC’s ‘Vigil’ Season 3 Teaser Sees Suranne Jones & Rose Leslie’s Detective Pair On An Artic Trek In Search Of Answers
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse English Football Giants Liverpool Confirm Sale Of Stake To Jeff Bezos & Facebook Co-Founder Eduardo Saverin Eurovision Eyes Voting Changes & Blocks Countries In “Armed Conflict” Zones From Hosting Competition Tom Prior Signs With Independent Creative Management View All August 17, 2026 2:29am Here’s your first look at Suranne Jones and Rose Leslie in Season 3 of BBC police drama Vigil . A teaser shows the pair trekking across a frozen tundra, long-range rifle strapped to their backs, as their latest high-stakes investigation takes them to a remote Arctic research station. “In the Arctic, you don’t understand what’s coming,” a foreboding voiceover says in the words spoken in the 25-second trailer. In Season 3 of the International Emmy-winning series, DCI Amy Silva (Jones) and DI Kirsten Longacre (Leslie) investigate why a member of a covert British special forces mission has been shot dead in the research station. Related Stories News BBC Seeks To Subpoena Ivanka Trump, Jared Kushner & Don Jr. In Defamation Lawsuit News Donald Trump Waging $10B Legal War Against BBC On Basis "Doctored" Documentary May Have Been Viewed 285 Times In America They need to both catch the killer and defuse a potential international confrontation, as different nations compete for control of the Arctic and its resources in the changing polar climate. Watch on Deadline The first two episodes will drop on Sunday, August 30 in the UK, with eps then running on Sunday and Monday nights at 9pm on BBC One. Season 3 cast includes Dominic Mafham, reprising his role as Sir Ian Downing, and new cast such as Jeppe Beck Laursen ( The Last Kingdom ) as Henrick Becken, Svalbard’s Chief of Police; Naomi Yang ( Under Salt Marsh ) Shen Jia, a microbiologist; Tornike Gogrichiani ( Extraction 2 ) as Fyodor, a Russian colonel; Steven Miller ( Dept. Q ) and Benjamin Wainwright( Maigret ) as Special Boat Service operators; Danusia Samal ( Red Eye ) as Jasmine Kelly, who works alongside Downing; Eric Godon (I n Bruges ) as Mayor Korotayev; and Amy Manson ( Rebus ) as Lorna McCallister, a geologist. Gary Lewis reprises his role as DSU Robertson, who continues to work closely with Amy and Kirsten. The six-part season comes from World Productions in association with its parent company, ITV Studios. Tom Edge is writer and creator, with additional writing coming from Tom Mair and Eve Hedderwick Turner. The producer is Marcus Wilson, associate producer is George Aza-Selinger and executive producers are Jake Lushington for World, Gaynor Holmes for the BBC and Edge. Stephanie Fyfe is the commissioning executive for the BBC, and the directors are Gareth Bryn and Faye Gilbert. ITV Studios handles the international distribution. Vigil Season 1, in which Jones’ Silva was enlisted to solve a murder on a navy submarine in Scottish waters, was BAFTA-nominated and won the International Emmy for Best Drama Series in 2021. Season 2, from 2023, focused on a deadly drone attack, launched to nearly nine million viewers and was in the BBC’s top-three most-watched dramas of the year. title: Diane Kruger & Dany Boon Are Nazi Hunters On The Trail Of Tim Roth’s Klaus Barbie In Netflix’s ‘Projet K’

Kruger and Boon will portray Beate and Serge Klarsfeld, the real-life husband-and-wife Nazi hunters. The couple spent years tracking down Nazis after the end of World War II. Famously, they pursued Klaus Barbie who was head of the Gestapo in Lyon. Responsible for the deaths of thousands of Jews, he became known as the ‘Butcher of Lyon’. title: In ‘Oasis,’ a School Spirals Into Violence – and Three Outcasts Take Refuge in a Forest (Exclusive Trailer)
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking Hayden Panettiere, Actress in ‘Heroes’ and ‘Nashville,’ Dies at 36 close By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 17, 2026 1:00am 'Oasis' Courtesy of Zeitgeist Filmproduktion Adolescent outcasts, identity and violence take center stage in Oasis ( Oase ), the much-anticipated debut feature of German writer-director Jannis Lenz, which will world premiere on Sept. 6 in the Horizons section of the 83rd edition of the Venice Film Festival . This one will be very different from that other Oasis movie at Venice, Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger , a concert documentary about the reunion tour of the famous band that brought Liam and Noel Gallagher back together. If you don’t believe me, just read this synopsis for Oasis . “When a viral video of a student threatening his classmates surfaces online, the school spirals into escalating violence,” it notes. “Crushed by the pressure of teachers and parents, three outcasts take refuge in a nearby forest. There, play hardens into ritual, and pain becomes an escape, until old wounds surface and the boundaries between them are redrawn.” Related Stories Locarno Open Doors Spotlight 2026 In 'A Vineyard for A Lobster,' Snowfall in a Ugandan Village Becomes a Political and Colonial Allegory Movies "It Was a Bumpy Ride!": Jack Rowan and Director Kieron J. Walsh on the Many Lives of Head-Bopping, Troubles-Set 'Skintown' The cinematic drama is an exploration of violence, body and identity – themes that Lenz has also touched on in his previous work. The cast stars up-and-coming German actors Florian Geißelmann ( Sound of Falling , Home Stories ), Anton Petzold ( Home Stories , Ouija ) and Mathilda Smidt ( Almania , Chabos ), as well as veteran Godehard Giese ( Rose , Transit , Babylon Berlin ). Britta Hammelstein ( Murder Mindfully , Woman of the Dead , The Sparrow in the Chimney ) and Ioana Iacob ( Do Not Expect Too Much From the End of the World ) also feature in the cast. Lenz directed Oasis based on a screenplay that he wrote with Alexander Dirninger, who also served as director of photography. The editors are Lenz and Melisa Krasniqi. “Body, space, and identity dissolve into one another, revealing the fragile beauty and quiet brutality of human relationships, while echoing the violence that shapes our contemporary world,” tease the press notes for Oasis . Check out the poster for the film, which THR can exclusively debut, right here. Lenz has previously turned heads with such shorts as Wannabe (2017), which got nominated for the European Film Award, and Soldat Ahmet (2021), which won several awards after its world premiere at the Visions du Réel festival in Switzerland. Oasis is produced by Germany’s Zeitgeist Filmproduktion and co-produced by Austria’s Wega Film and Germany’s Third Picture in collaboration with We Fade to Grey, Ocean Pictures Filmproduktion and Totem Films. The German theatrical release is planned for February 2027 via Mindjazz Pictures. Totem is handling international sales on the German-Austrian co-production. THR can now also exclusively premiere a trailer for the movie. School scenes, one pupil getting questioned about his threat of violence against schoolmates, and images of the protagonists in the forest create unsettling atmosphere. Oh yeah, there are also disturbing drawings. All in all, the audiovisual atmosphere teased here feels unnerving. But check out the trailer for Oasis yourself right here. THR

The show, supported by Netflix, is set for Sept. 20 at the Southbank Centre’s Royal Festival Hall in London. The new names joining the lineup include chart-topper Sophie Ellis-Bextor, BAFTA Breakthrough Brit Susan Wokoma (“Enola Holmes”), leading dramatist James Graham (“Dear England”), Daniel Ings (“The Gentleman”), Calam Lynch (“Rings of Power”), Fay Ripley (“Cold Feet”), Rhea Norwood (“Heartstopper”) and Megan Bolton (TikTok comedian). The show will be powered on stage, behind the scenes and on screen by young talent nurtured through Netflix and National Youth Theatre’s “Ignite Your Creativity” program. NYT patron Sophie Ellis-Bextor said: “I’m proud to be a Patron of the National Youth Theatre, which gave me a great confidence boost as a young person and continues to do the same for thousands of young performers around the country.” Wokoma added: “NYT shaped everything for me… I learned how to be a good company member and it’s absolutely one of my strengths as an actor and writer. It’s the way you learn and grow and surprise yourself.” Ings said: “A lot of the people I’m closest to today are friends I made at NYT, and it shaped the way I approach acting and being part of a company. That being said, I have a lot to say to my younger self, so I can’t wait to be back with the NYT this September for a night to remember.” Lynch added: “I’m looking forward to returning to my NYT roots for a special evening celebrating seventy years of youth theatre.” Bolton said: “NYT is where I started my performing journey and is a company that means a lot to me. I’m looking forward to joining some amazing talent on stage for an evening to remember.” Netflix has backed National Youth Theatre since 2023 through a partnership that has generated more than 4,000 free places aimed at steering young people toward behind-the-scenes creative careers. The charity points to its alumni roster as evidence that a majority of the U.K.’s top screen talent got their start in theater. That roster includes Daniel Craig, Helen Mirren, Adeel Akhtar, Andrea Riseborough, Matt Smith, Regé-Jean Page and Susan Wokoma, along with dramatists Jack Thorne, James Graham, Miriam Battye, Lennie James and Sarah Solemani, comedians Tom Allen and Joel Dommett, and musicians Ed Sheeran and Sophie Ellis-Bextor. Tickets for “Letters to My Younger Future Self” are on sale now, with proceeds benefiting the national charity in its 70th anniversary year. National Youth Theatre named Netflix as headline sponsor of the event, with additional backing from Arts Council England and Eon Productions. title: ‘Snapshot’ Review: A Nifty Calling-Card Debut Refashions the Jack the Ripper Story as Found-Footage Horror
full_text: Aug 17, 2026 12:59am PT ‘Snapshot’ Review: A Nifty Calling-Card Debut Refashions the Jack the Ripper Story as Found-Footage Horror Director Joseph Archer and screenwriter-star Cathy Wippell will turn heads with this undeniably stunt-y but eerie novelty set in Victorian London and shot as though with a pinhole camera. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘Snapshot’ Review: A Nifty Calling-Card Debut Refashions the Jack the Ripper Story as Found-Footage Horror 1 hour ago ‘Mission’ Review: An All-In George MacKay Performance Anchors a Fevered Mental Illness Portrait 19 hours ago ‘The State of Us’ Review: A Pair of Spirited Performances Lift a Familiar Yorkshire Tearjerker 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Silicon Gothic Found footage may be a fairly stale gimmick in horror these days, but the low-budget British indie “ Snapshot ” finds a way to freshen up the idea — and if that largely amounts to layering another technical gimmick over it, the results are nonetheless striking. Emulating the look of 19th-century pinhole photography, with the entire film presented in a circular 1:1 aspect ratio, this resourceful debut feature from director Joseph Archer and screenwriter-star Cathy Wippell turns the visual restrictions of that device to its advantage: This imagining of the well-trodden Jack the Ripper tale hinges heavily on what can’t be seen, as it follows a group of young Victorian women pursuing their own supernatural theory behind the killings terrorizing London, and the pioneering male filmmaker who takes it upon himself to document their efforts. Related Stories Hollywood Failed Hayden Panettiere Hayden Panettiere, 'Heroes' and 'Scream' Star, Dies at 36 Viewers must swallow a certain degree of contrivance to go along with “Snapshot.” For one thing, it demands we accept that Tamworth (voiced by “All My Friends Hate Me” star Tom Stourton), the heard-but-not-seen inventor behind the camera, could have assumed a near fly-on-the-wall kind of presence in various unseemly locations through east London’s underbelly to have captured these revealingly candid reels. (Complete with leagues-ahead-its-time sound-recording technology, to boot.) Popular on Variety Introductory text informs us that this footage was discovered languishing in the (fictitious) “British Film Archive,” and Archer, also the film’s editor, deftly maintains a jumpy structural sense of reels rather crudely sequenced, with telling gaps between them. As DP, his visual approximation of early-cinema techniques, often wittily distressed, sometimes betrays his contemporary ones; the actors, likewise, slip in and out of period register. Still, if its illusion isn’t entirely complete, “Snapshot” is nonetheless an effectively eerie novelty, sure to attract attention in arthouse horror circles following its competition premiere in Edinburgh. Its next stop will be London’s genre-specific FrightFest later this month, but international festival programmers should take an interest too. The morbidly lilting music-hall staple “Two Lovely Black Eyes” (“Only for telling a man he was wrong,” runs the follow-up lyric) recurs throughout “Snapshot,” becoming the defining musical theme in a story of female exploitation and exasperation in a society not yet rocked by the women’s suffrage movement. Tamworth, evidently a young man, appears sympathetic to the cause, spending much time in female company to chronicle the reality of their lives outside the sphere of patriarchal influence; still, as the film continues, the palpable shadow of the male gaze on proceedings becomes unnervingly hard to shake. His key subjects include Minnie (Wippell, writing herself the juiciest role here), an intrepid, rebellious type who’s also something of a class tourist: Though raised in a well-to-do London family, she prefers to hang out with the sex workers and miscreants of the city’s working-class East End, where her close friend Fanny (Hazel Rogers) practices the oldest profession in the care of maternal madam Evelyn (Nadia Lamin). Of late, women like Fanny have been turning up dead in the area’s backstreets with alarming frequency; a climate of terror is setting in as the Ripper’s body count rises, but there’s still a living to be made. In any case, Minnie and Fanny — along with other women in their circle — have become convinced that the killer is actually a phantom entity, and are determined to hunt the ghost down by patrolling his spooked environs and making spiritual contact with his dead victims — with Tamworth, of course, reliably on hand to make a permanent record of this plainly doomed project. As “Snapshot” becomes a queasily sustained exercise in waiting for the penny to drop, Archer and Wippell keep the story lean and the overt scares sparse, instead cultivating a more subtly pervading mood of disquiet and dread that aims to honor the everyday experience of women in this particular milieu. “Snapshot” does risk feeling more like a very clever exercise than a fully realized narrative: Even with a tight 86-minute running time, the drama begins to spin its wheels a bit in the second half, while the characters have limited room to grow in this confined formal setup. But the payoff is mordantly effective, and the film’s fine sense of gallows humor gives it some welcome tonal breadth. It promises bigger, even more ambitious things from Archer, Wippell and their production outfit Silicon Gothic, and stakes out a commitment to horror filmmaking that doesn’t merely chase Hollywood trends, instead using both the resources and the cultural baggage on their doorstep. ‘Snapshot’ Review: A Nifty Calling-Card Debut Refashions the Jack the Ripper Story as Found-Footage Horror Reviewed at Soho Screening Rooms, London, July 30, 2026. Executive producers: Mickey Andro, Chippy Babu, Michael Osowski, Suresh Cedrick Pereira, Tushar Rakheja, Mario Stefan, Megan Teo, Barry Vonk. Crew: Director, camera, editor: Joseph Archer. The project is among the 15 titles selected for the 2026 Europe-Latin America Co-Production Forum at the San Sebastián Film Festival. Its San Sebastián berth comes as Zoe Films builds a growing festival presence. The Italian company has Ali Asgari’s “A Bit of Light” in competition at the Venice Film Festival and Shawn Garry’s “After Elena,” starring Alfredo Castro, heading to Toronto’s Centrepiece section. Related Stories Hayden Panettiere, 'Heroes' and 'Scream' Star, Dies at 36 Hollywood Failed Hayden Panettiere The move brings producer Alejandro Saevich into a production team comprising Zoe Films’ Lorenzo Cioffi and Giampà and Fiasco’s Elena Fortes. Madrefoca, co-founded in 2023 by Saevich, is also behind Nathalia Acevedo’s “Salón de Belleza,” selected for competition at Venice Days this year. Popular on Variety Written by Giampà with Melissa Nocetti, “Isabel Hernández” follows a young agronomist living in the Guatemalan jungle who recognizes the father who abandoned her as a child in a documentary about Latin American migrants in the U.S. Her search for answers leads to two men recently deported by ICE who knew him: a young man whom her father raised like a son and a former soldier who claims to know the secret behind his disappearance. Their conflicting accounts force Isabel to confront a past shaped by Guatemala’s civil war and fractured memories of the man she barely knew. “Isabel tries to piece together the past, claim a future of her own, find her own peace,” Giampà said. The film grows out of seven years of research Giampà carried out in Guatemala, living with forest communities and spending time with Mayan survivors of the genocidal massacres of the 1980s, former guerrillas and people deported from the U.S. by ICE. Giampà plans to work largely with non-professional actors “whose own lives resonate with the story,” extending the film’s research-driven approach into its casting. Shooting is planned for autumn 2027. “Isabel Hernández” is part of TorinoFilmLab FeatureLab 2026, previously participated in the EAVE Producers Workshop 2025 and has received development support from Film Commission Regione Campania. Founded in 2023, Zoe Films’ previous productions include Asgari’s “Divine Comedy,” selected for Venice Horizons in 2025, and Alessandro Cassigoli and Casey Kauffman’s “Vittoria,” which played Venice Horizons Extra in 2024. Its short-film slate includes Giampà’s “Astronauta,” selected for Clermont-Ferrand’s 2026 International Competition, and Mel Nocetti’s “I Used to Call That Man Home,” which played Rotterdam earlier this year. The 2026 Europe-Latin America Co-Production Forum will run Sept. 21-23 as part of the 74th San Sebastián Film Festival, which takes place Sept. 18-26. title: Kenneth Branagh On Moving From Shakespeare To Action-Comedy In ‘Mayday’: “I Thought Zach Galifianakis Should Play The Part, But I Was Very Pleased They Asked Me” – Edinburgh Film Festival
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Damon Wise Damon Wise Film Editor, Awards yo_damo More Stories By Damon ‘Douglas Gordon By Douglas Gordon’ Director Finlay Pretsell On His Portrait Of An Eccentric Genius: “This Is The Mind Of A Conceptual Artist” – Edinburgh Film Festival ‘Borges And Me’ Review: Marc Turtletaub’s Hallucinatory ’70s Road Trip Is Smart, Literary And Playful – Edinburgh Film Festival Ewan McGregor: The Actor Opens Up About His Career, His Return To Scotland & Taking A Chance With Obi-Wan: “Deciding To Do ‘Star Wars’ Was Hard” – Edinburgh Film Festival View All August 17, 2026 12:12am Kenneth Branagh and Ryan Reynolds in 'Mayday' courtesy of Apple Actor-director Kenneth Branagh arrived in Edinburgh to accept the festival’s inaugural Outstanding Contribution to Cinema award from festival director Paul Ridd and immediately joked that he would break it up into little pieces. “Actually, I wouldn’t,” he told the audience, “but if I did, I would give to you , and I’m not just being sappy. Certainly, the reason why I’m standing here is that because over the last number of years, so many of you have been kind enough to support the films that we do and that are celebrated here at the festival. It just wouldn’t be possible to be working in this industry without appreciative audiences who take a risk and who spend their cash and invest their time.” Related Stories Festivals 'Douglas Gordon By Douglas Gordon' Director Finlay Pretsell On His Portrait Of An Eccentric Genius: "This Is The Mind Of A Conceptual Artist" - Edinburgh Film Festival Festivals 'Borges And Me' Review: Marc Turtletaub's Hallucinatory '70s Road Trip Is Smart, Literary And Playful - Edinburgh Film Festival Speaking to The Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw, Branagh discussed his 40-year career in movies both as an actor and director, having screened his 1989 debut Henry V . The event began, however, with an entertaining sample of his upcoming Apple film Mayday , an ‘80s-set action film in which he plays a disillusioned KGB agent who teams up with a US Navy pilot ( Ryan Reynolds ) who is stranded behind enemy lines. Watch on Deadline Branagh was full of praise for writer-directors, Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley. “You may know their work from Game Night and Dungeons & Dragons ,” he said, “both films of deceptive ease. Really entertaining, popular movies that are very cannily done. They had planned all the action and the style sequences, so the invitation was for me to step up and enact their imagination. They’re both excellent directors, but I find it terrific to be directed by two directors. They can gang up on you in a really good way, in a helpful way. “I read the script in one sitting,” he recalled. “I was in an airport, during a long delay in coming back home. And I remember thinking, ‘This knows exactly what it’s meant to be. It’s grasp of the period and its sheer desire to entertain — but with a lot of very skillful touches — is great. Why the hell are they asking me to be in?’ I thought Zach Galifianakis should play the part actually, but I was very pleased they asked me.” Since the part he’s playing is Russian, Bradshaw asked if he would consider playing Vladimir Putin. “It depends on the writing,” said Branagh. “But it also depends on whether you feel that somehow, you can serve [the role] appropriately. But there’s no question that such characters, for all the reasons we’re all too familiar with, are riveting. I guess it’s pretty important to analyze, investigate and understand how and why, in as much as we can draw inferences from what little we know of the inner lives and inner machinations of such regimes, how these people operate. He’s a figure that dominates our experience in many ways, along with a number of other key figures. So just like Shakespeare wrote about all those people in control of the power in our lives, he’s a creature that fascinates us, and from whom we might learn something in the investigation.” Branagh went on to say that his next project was a little more traditional, given his theatrical background, being a documentary about the history of British theater in the 20th century. “It’s directed by a young British actor, Freddie Fox ,” he said. “You may know him from numerous pieces of work and movies, but most recently Slow Horses . He has incredible access to a number of significant people across that period. He particularly focuses on what made the impact of the theater, socially, and the change that it spoke about — whether it was to do with LGBTQ rights or the political situation in Northern Ireland, et cetera — but it also contains a really keen interest in performance.” ‘Nashville’ & ‘Heroes’ Star Hayden Panettiere Dies At 36; Career In Photos Depp In Talks For ‘Pirates 6,’ Bruckheimer Says; Disney Poised For Huge 2028: Analysis 2nd Fastest To $2B Global; $70M Third Frame; Dino Movies At $20M+ In U.S. ‘Call Her Daddy’ Host Alex Cooper In Talks With CAA After UTA Exit Under Cloud Read More About: Comments

title: ‘Douglas Gordon By Douglas Gordon’ Director Finlay Pretsell On His Portrait Of An Eccentric Genius: “This Is The Mind Of A Conceptual Artist” – Edinburgh Film Festival
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Damon Wise Damon Wise Film Editor, Awards yo_damo More Stories By Damon ‘Douglas Gordon By Douglas Gordon’ Director Finlay Pretsell On His Portrait Of An Eccentric Genius: “This Is The Mind Of A Conceptual Artist” – Edinburgh Film Festival ‘Borges And Me’ Review: Marc Turtletaub’s Hallucinatory ’70s Road Trip Is Smart, Literary And Playful – Edinburgh Film Festival Ewan McGregor: The Actor Opens Up About His Career, His Return To Scotland & Taking A Chance With Obi-Wan: “Deciding To Do ‘Star Wars’ Was Hard” – Edinburgh Film Festival View All August 16, 2026 11:20pm ‘Douglas Gordon By Douglas Gordon’ EIFF On the face of it, Finlay Pretsell’s first feature, Time Trial (2017), seemed like any other underdog sports movie, chronicling the last hurrah of disgraced Scottish cyclist David Millar in his last year as a professional rider at the Tour De France. Others might have taken the easy option and milked this against-all-odds story for dramatic tension, but Pretsell chose instead to focus on the complex mass of confidence and insecurity that lay behind Millar’s public image — the question it asks is not whether Millar will defy the odds and win, but can he survive a loss? His new film Douglas Gordon By Douglas Gordon is just as insightful, a portrait of the Scottish artist behind such works as 24 Hour Psycho — Hitchcock’s film slowed down to one frame per half a second — and Zidane: A 21st Century Portrait , in which 17 cameras tracked the course of a football match by focusing on a single player. As the title suggests, Gordon was not a passive subject, actively fighting his director for authorship of the story. The result is a fascinating deconstruction of the documentary process, with Pretsell both charmed and exasperated by his mercurial and temperamental subject. Related Stories Festivals 'Borges And Me' Review: Marc Turtletaub's Hallucinatory '70s Road Trip Is Smart, Literary And Playful - Edinburgh Film Festival Festivals Ewan McGregor: The Actor Opens Up About His Career, His Return To Scotland & Taking A Chance With Obi-Wan: "Deciding To Do 'Star Wars' Was Hard" - Edinburgh Film Festival DEADLINE: Did you know Douglas Gordon’s work beforehand? Watch on Deadline FINLAY PRETSELL: Yes. He was the biggest inspiration to set me on the journey to make films, to be honest. I saw Zidane: A 21st Century Portrait while I was attempting to make a cycling film and I wanted it to be something else. I wanted it to be experiential . I saw Zidane and it blew me away in its ability to take me onto the pitch. Then I met him. I was kind of blown away by his generosity. DEADLINE: When did you first meet him? PRETSELL: It was 20 years ago, here at the Edinburgh Film Festival , funnily enough. And he just stood and talked to me and he was so warm and generous and interested and sort of empowered me to do what I wanted to do. Not pretentious, not standoffish, not too busy. I think that’s what I really liked about him. I saw this amazing character. He was so comical, there was something behind the eyes, behind this very Glaswegian accent. There was something about him that made me think, “Oh, this isn’t what I expected.” Artists are generally sort of quiet and introverted, but there was some sort of… not danger about him, exactly, but there was something going on that was exciting and intriguing. I didn’t think about making a film about him then, but we stayed in touch by email. And then during COVID, I said, “Look, are you up for doing something together?” I heard nothing back. I thought, “OK, whatever, fine.” And then out of the blue, I got a call from Berlin. A Scottish accent. I didn’t know who it was. It was Douglas. “So, what are we going to do?” he said. “Film? Fiction? Drama? Series? Episodic?” From then on, we just started talking, and it took me probably about a year to finally get into his studio, during which time I would record our conversations that we were having. It became this kind of confessional thing, because I’d get him at all times of the day: First thing in the morning, or in the afternoon, or late at night, I was recording our conversations. I never really thought I’d ever use them. But in the end, we used them quite a lot. and it became quite critical to the arc of the film. DEADLINE: How do you start a project like this? Do you just start filming and see what happens? PRETSELL: Sort of. I’m quite slow, in a way, at coming up with an idea. I think I saw various scenes in my head, but I have to be in the room with someone to really understand things and start to work it all out. I can’t just make something up and say, “Right, this is what I want to do.” But in my head I thought, “This is an experience of a successful working artist, and I want to capture this somehow.” I want to be a fly in the wall. DEADLINE: Were you looking for moments in the life of an artist then? PRETSELL : Yeah. The thing with Douglas is that he let us into something deeply personal. But he had to do it when he was ready to let us in, and it was really difficult to pin him down. I just had to let go [of the reins], and he would sort of deliver a performance of what he thought I would want to know about him, which was just amazing. Thematically, it runs all the way through the film. He’s in charge. Initially, I would always try and control everything, and I would get quite frustrated — as you see in the film — and he would get frustrated with me. But I realized that there was no other way, and I think it was that relinquishing of control that was essential to make the project work and not get too concerned with my own ego getting burnt all the time. DEADLINE: When did you realize he wasn’t going to give anything away? Because people might go to this film thinking, “Why did he make 24 Hour Psycho ? Why did he make Zidane ?” What would you say to those people if they think that’s what they’re going to get? PRETSELL: I would tell them, this is the mind that created them. And him explaining it would make it no clearer to anyone. Watching the film will explain it in a non-didactic way, I suppose. This is the mind of a conceptual artist. Too much context, I think, kills many documentaries. People feel like they’re forced to contextualize absolutely everything in docs, and I’m like, why are we not allowed just to be a bit freer with these narratives? It’s not about being smart or holding something back, I just want to create an experience. As soon as you’re giving facts and dates, it starts to get in the way of the experience, or the feeling of what it is that he does. As he says in the film, ambiguity is what it’s all about. Not that the film itself should be ambiguous, necessarily, but you ask yourself, “Is he acting? Is he telling the truth? Are we seeing the real Douglas Gordon now?” Who cares! We’re telling a story, and he’s part of that story. He’s a performer. DEADLINE: So, it becomes another artwork to hang next to the others? PRETSELL: Yeah, exactly. It sort of does. But what I can say is that everything he did for us was authentic. It’s from him, and a;; these beautiful moments he would just produce out of nowhere. It wasn’t like we’d say, “Maybe we should talk about your mum now. Maybe we should talk about…” It would just come out. I’d often email him some points before we talked, and if we managed to do get to of these points, great. But if not, it didn’t matter. Something better would happen. DEADLINE: Is there ever a chance he could have just walked away and destroyed the project? PRETSELL : Oh, of course. Totally. I was thinking that all along, because I could imagine him doing just that. He doesn’t need me. He doesn’t need a film about him. It was in the back of my mind the whole time. But I never give up in these situations. I’m like, “No, no, no. We are going to make this film.” So, yeah, of course, he could have absolutely walked away at any point. It’d be much easier for him not having us around, to have me not calling him up all the time, but he likes that discussion, that discourse. DEADLINE: What did you learn about conceptual art? PRETSELL: Oh God, I don’t know. Nothing. [Laughs.] I think what I learned is that everything is grist to the mill. All these discussions we would have around his kitchen table, he would write them on the walls all over his studio. That made me realize that everything could be turned into an artwork, in a way. title: Hollywood Failed Hayden Panettiere
full_text: Aug 16, 2026 11:03pm PT Hollywood Failed Hayden Panettiere By Marlow Stern Plus Icon Marlow Stern Chief Correspondent Latest John Oliver Brutally Mocks Trump for Sacrificing Staff in Airplane-Swap Incident 6 hours ago Matthew McConaughey’s First Screen Role Helped Catch a Murderer 2 days ago Shannon Elizabeth’s Long, Bumpy Road to OnlyFans Stardom 4 days ago See All Getty Images Hayden Panettiere , the former child actress who grew up onscreen before our very eyes, passed away Sunday at the age of 36 . She died five days before her 37th birthday. “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden,” her father Alan said in a statement. “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen.” Related Stories Box Office: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Swings into Second Weekend With $43 Million on Friday Korea Box Office: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Captures 81% Market Share in Colossal Debut While we are still awaiting a cause of death, Panettiere, who delivered her breakthrough performance at the age of 10 in “Remember the Titans” before starring in the NBC superhero saga “Heroes,” as fan favorite Kirby Reed in the “Scream” films and Juliette Barnes in the country music drama “Nashville,” had struggled for years battling drug addiction, alcoholism and depression, and suffered mightily at the hands of Hollywood. Panettiere chronicled her Hollywood highs and lows in her eye-opening memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning,” released May 19 of this year. Popular on Variety In the prologue to her book, she mentions the five stages of grief — and her belief in a sixth, floated by the author David Kessler in his book “Finding Meaning.” That stage is meaning, and Panettiere wrote that “my traumas have offered me meaning through a sense of humor, some ridiculous stories, prioritizing my health, a deeper relationship with my parents, pets I adore, animal rights and environmentalism that gives me purpose, and now, this book.” She continued: “All the heartaches I’ve endured have allowed me to come to a place of empathy and understanding for everything my loved ones have come up against and — most importantly — for myself. They’ve also given me determination. I’m like Dory, the resilient little fish in ‘Finding Nemo,’ who ‘just keeps swimming’ even when she comes face-to-face with a bunch of sharks.” Raised in Palisades, New York, Panettiere landed a series of commercials — the first at only 11 months old — before landing a role in the soap opera “One Life to Live” at the age of 5. She described herself as a “willful child” who wouldn’t be bossed around; a “tomboy” with a big head of curly hair and a “spunky, sassy attitude.” There are plenty of bright moments in her book, like the time she tossed a football around with Denzel Washington on the set of “Remember the Titans” — a movie-making experience she called “the happiest I’d ever felt as an actor” — and disappointing ones, such as losing a role in “Panic Room” to Kristen Stewart after Nicole Kidman backed out of the film due to injury. She shared intimate details about her family life, like the time her mom discovered her father was having an affair and the destructive impact it had on their family dynamic; her complicated relationship with her stage-mom mother, a former soap opera actress; and being overcome with grief after losing her beloved brother and confidant, Jansen, to heart complications in 2023. But the moments from “This Is Me: A Reckoning” that stuck with me the most concerned the many ways she was targeted by Hollywood predators. There was the “important executive at NBC” who kissed her on the lips at a party in 2008 while she starred on his network’s hit show “Heroes,” or the time that a star-studded apartment party in Los Feliz took a turn for the appalling when an “Oscar-winning actor and director” cornered a 19-year-old Panettiere as she was about to leave and tricked her into looking at his exposed testicles with the line, “There’s a big wad of gum on my pants.” “I looked down and recoiled,” she recalled in the book. “This well-respected, award-winning actor’s testicles were hanging out from his unzipped fly… Up to that moment, men in Hollywood had always been kind and respectful around me. There may have been a peck on the lips here and an inappropriate comment there, but nothing had crossed a line.” And that line kept getting crossed, again and again. One of the most shocking incidents occurred when Panettiere was 18 and an actress friend, who she calls Stella in the book, invited her to a yacht party in the South of France. Stella ushered her down into the bowels of the ship and to a cabin where a “famous 30-something British singer-songwriter” lay naked in bed, his bottom half covered in sheets. “I want you to get in bed with him. He has a huge dick,” Stella told Panettiere, who subsequently panicked, writing, “My thoughts were a blur, but I’d spent my life trusting that others had my best interests at heart. Being ‘managed’ was routine, to the point where I lost faith in my intuition. I could feel my heart pounding. As I settled in underneath the sheets, I disassociated. My body no longer felt like my own.” Then, her “survival instinct kicked in” and she managed to escape before anything happened. The Hollywood crowd proved so off-putting to Panettiere that she found herself drawn to the former heavyweight champion boxer Wladimir Klitschko, who is currently helping defend his country of Ukraine against Russia’s invasion, because of how un-Hollywood he is. The two share a daughter, Kaya. As Panettiere told People , when she was only 15, someone on her team began plying her with “happy pills” before she walked red carpets. “They were to make me peppy during interviews,” Panettiere said. “I had no idea that this was not an appropriate thing, or what door that would open for me when it came to my addiction… As I got older, the drugs and alcohol became something I almost couldn’t live without.” Her battle with drugs, alcohol and depression led to an eight-month rehab stint in 2020, where she wrote candidly about the painful effects of withdrawal on her body and mind. “As my nervous system tried to regulate itself without the depressant effects of alcohol, it went into overdrive, and my whole body shook, I couldn’t sleep, and my head pounded like it was pressing against my skull… A doctor told me that if I didn’t stop drinking, I’d be dead within five years,” she recalled in her book. Whatever her cause of death is, one thing is certain: Hollywood failed to protect Hayden Panettiere. Hopefully, her death will serve as a reminder to the industry’s powers that be that young girls and women need to be heard, need to feel safe, and need to be shielded from its more sordid characters. I’ll leave you with a portion of the final chapter of Panettiere’s memoir, which she named “One Final Thought”: “Radical acceptance has taught me to walk hand in hand with my triumphs and my tragedies because they’ve made me who I am. And today, I really love that person. If there’s anything I can offer you with this book, it’s my hope that you do the same.” Miley Cyrus Says She ‘Genuinely’ Wants to Act Again as She Signs With Atlantic Records and Charts Next Chapter: ‘I’d Love to Disappear Into Something Romantic’ Loading comments... And we haven’t even seen him fully train the Green Lantern’s back-up guardian for Earth, Aaron Pierre’s John Stewart. On tonight’s special episode of Crew Call , Lanterns co-creators and EPs Chris Mundy , Tom King , and Damon Lindelof unpack that shocker ending for Jordan, and how and why the trio teamed up to revive Green Lantern for the new DC under James Gunn and Peter Safran. That’s when he appears as a digital carbon copy (or “back-up”) to Stewart following the latter’s survival from a car-crash. That was a major tip-off as to how tonight’s episode would end. Why did Mundy, King and Lindelof leave a breadcrumb? Listen below. The older Green Lantern taunted the alien so much, that the creature detonated itself, blowing a hole into the side of the jail. Greg Berlanti co-wrote that movie, and he tried to revive the property for Warner Bros TV before Green Lantern glowed into Lanterns . title: ‘Love Story’ Producers Didn’t Expect Carolyn Bessette’s TikTok Fan Army to Come for Them
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking Hayden Panettiere, Actress in ‘Heroes’ and ‘Nashville,’ Dies at 36 close By Mikey O'Connell Plus Icon Mikey O'Connell Senior Entertainment Editor View All August 16, 2026 12:30pm Paul Anthony Kelly and Sarah Pidgeon in FX’s Love Story FX Catalog the ways in which Love Story : John F. Kennedy Jr. & Carolyn Bessette could have gone wrong, and the tally might rival a Thanksgiving grocery list. Pressure on capturing the tragic couple and their time period was high enough before early test photos sent devotees of Bessette’s style into a tizzy and a legion of paparazzi to the FX limited series’ Manhattan shoot. But Love Story ultimately prevailed, commandeering online discourse for its nine-episode run and fetching seven Emmy nominations — including top limited series, one for lead actress Sarah Pidgeon and, shutting down any sartorial naysayers, outstanding period costumes. Power producing duo Nina Jacobson and Brad Simpson know they could make things easier on themselves, but, like with their previous historic collaborations with Ryan Murphy, the fun is in trying to capture a feeling on camera that’s no longer found in real life. Related Stories TV 'DTF St. Louis' Creator Steven Conrad Has No Plans to Make More Movies TV 'The Pitt' Showrunner Admits Season One's Notoriety Amped Up Pressure For Season Two: "We Had to Prove That It Wasn't Just a Fluke" Each true story brings a different minefield to navigate in terms of what’s verifiable information, what’s unknown and the varying public sentiments. Which needle was the most difficult to thread on Love Story ? NINA JACOBSON It’s about understanding both what was known about them and what was not known for so many people. Because, when we were growing up, they were like American royalty. They were icons. But with the subsequent generations, what we found is that people knew her so much better than they knew him. She had become a posthumous influencer. Yet, as much as people knew of her, it was only visual. It didn’t really have anything to do with who she was as a person. BRAD SIMPSON There were lots of recordings of him. He’d get tons of interviews. He was very public. We had to find her voice based on descriptions. And we just knew from all the research that, even though she presented as this WASP ideal and a sort of distant figure, she was incredibly warm and funny. Bringing that to life was one of our biggest challenges. Were you aware of how substantial the Carolyn fan accounts on Instagram and TikTok were? SIMPSON No, but we did know that she’d become this avatar for quiet luxury. Often, when we would get costume designers presenting us styles for actresses in our movies and TV shows, she would appear again and again on wardrobe boards. And we did know that there was a lot on TikTok about her, but we didn’t know how fevered it was when those early photos leaked and the world rained down saying it was going to be a disaster. It showed us the depth of the reach to people who weren’t even alive when she was around. I think you’ve been vindicated by a lot of the aesthetics. How did you capture ’90s New York without going wildly over budget? SIMPSON New York has changed so much more than we’d realized since the 1990s. It’s much easier to shoot period in L.A. New York has huge glass skyscrapers everywhere. There are bike lanes in the streets. It was a city that always stayed the same, and now it looks very different. Luckily, the places that were our main locations, Tribeca and the Upper East Side, had really stayed the same. I recognized quite a few restaurants, too. SIMPSON We were lucky that some of the iconic restaurants that they visited — Indochine, The Odeon, Bubby’s — are still there. We managed to shoot the last surviving restaurant of Sixth Street’s India row [Panna II], which has now been swarmed with people. We were lucky in that some of those places just have that same great aesthetic, but [our production designer] Alex DiGerlando worked really hard with our locations department to find places that looked right and gave us a sense of New York during that time. On a show like The Shards , we’re doing an interpretation of 1981. People wanted Love Story to evoke a well-photographed time. From what I’ve seen of The Shards , it looks very 1980s. Do you two ever do anything that’s just contemporary and easy? SIMPSON Back on [ The People v. O.J. Simpson: American Crime Story ], we didn’t understand. When we got into TV, we were naive. Our first script of O.J. had 110 scenes in it, and I remember the first visual production executive was like, “This is unshootable. There are no standing sets.” You’d think we would’ve learned that lesson by now, which is to write to standing sets and not have so many scenes, but we tend to gravitate toward stories that are a little bit historical and feel cinematic. JACOBSON We came to television as feature producers. So, on the one hand, we’ve learned along the way that a TV show is not just a long movie. There are some tricks to the trade. But at the same time, partly because we tend to alternate between books and historic stories, there’s an ambition to try to capture a feeling. You can never make a book adaptation feel just like the book, but evoking the feeling you had when you read the book or the feeling you had about real people or time, that is our north star. We like having something to try to honor, preserve, capture, embody and get right as an organizing principle in a way that feels honest, even when you take the liberties you have to take in order to tell any story. Looking at each of the eight episodes of Love Story , which was the hardest one to pull off — either logistically or tonally? SIMPSON Everything’s difficult. Even a show that doesn’t work is difficult to pull off. ( Laughs .) But one challenging one was episode eight, “Exit Strategy,” which is just the two of them in a loft as their marriage is falling apart. Ryan had always had an idea to do a bottle episode to show the tensions in the marriage. But that episode proved to be a real challenge — in a great way because we were stripped of all the clothes and other characters. It had to move us through their relationship. The writers, Connor Hines and Juli Weiner, treated it as if it was a play. We rehearsed the actors on weekends and constantly rewrote. Logistically, the hardest episode to pull off was “The Wedding.” We had to live up to the romance and re-create Georgia. And then, of course, the finale. There was the question of how much to show the plane crash, of how to be respectful while giving people the information they need and honoring what the characters went through. It’s been a few months now since the series aired. Has any feedback trickled to you from anyone surrounding the Kennedy camp? JACOBSON No, the Kennedys have not called recently. ( Laughs .) SIMPSON So much has been written about them. They’ve been documented in so many ways. We fell in love with all these characters and wanted to be respectful and make something that was a tribute. As a family, it must be hard to live in a public life. It’s part of what our show is about. But no, nothing has trickled back to us. Looking at a lot of your collaborations with Ryan — Crime Story, Sports Story and Love Story — how do you approach them at this point? How actively are you trying to identify stories that would fit in those franchises? JACOBSON We’re always looking. We’re like truffle pigs, constantly sniffing to find the next thing. What we tend to do is identify a few, put them into the works and wait for something to be good enough to be worth making. That doesn’t always happen at the rate at which we would like. SIMPSON I look at the way we produce as if we’re curating our own magazine. I grew up with Tina Brown’s Vanity Fair . I can imagine Crazy Rich Asians as an article about the rise of Chinese money and the culture of Singapore. You can imagine Pose as a feature about the trans ballroom scene. Every American Crime Story would obviously would fit in. I almost think of ourselves as editors, hoping stories come in well as journalists try to crack them. title: Karol G Brings Vibrant Vibes to Los Angeles With Her Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking Hayden Panettiere, Actress in ‘Heroes’ and ‘Nashville,’ Dies at 36 close By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 16, 2026 12:24pm Karol G performs during the first of three nights headlining the SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, on Aug. 14, 2026, for her Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour. Jill Connelly/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Coming off of her history-making Coachella headlining set, Karol G had an opportunity to bring the Latin love to the global stage with her Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour, and she did just that. She delivered an extended version of her festival set during the first of three shows at Inglewood’s SoFi Stadium on Friday night, as the 35-year-old Colombian singer-songwriter had the sold-out crowd on their feet, dancing from the second she appeared on the tropical-inspired stage to the final moment when she said her goodbyes. After emerging from a three-story stone cave structure at the top of the stage, which is a nod to the landscape and prehistoric caves of her native Colombia, she kicked off the show with electrifying vibes, first performing her fan-favorite song “Latina Foreva.” Wearing a gold sequin look, surrounded by backup dancers, she set the tone for what’s to come. The night’s vibes were also set when veteran actor Edward James Olmos — who starred in the 1997 film Selena , based on the life of the late Tejano icon, whom Karol G has called her lifelong idol — told the audience in a video message, “Nights like this don’t happen by chance. Karol G then slowed things down a bit with tracks from her newly released sixth studio album, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto , which is an emotional and moody shift from the high-energy Tropicoqueta vibes. During night one, she brought out Cigarettes After Sex frontman Greg Gonzalez to perform their new song, “Después de Ti.” Act three continued to be a standout moment during night two on Saturday, when Bruno Mars also made a surprise cameo to perform his and Karol G’s new song “Still,” as well as record the music video. #KarolG performs new song “Después de ti” with Cigarettes After Sex frontman Greg Gonzalez during night one of Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour in L.A. pic.twitter.com/3iQxnB93Nx — The Hollywood Reporter (@THR) August 15, 2026 The energy was later brought back up, getting fans back on their feet, when Karol G and her dancers started making their way to the illuminated stone pool on the B-stage. The love and appreciation that Karol G has for her fans was on full display ahead of the show’s final act, as she took several moments to interact with them. From taking photos to sharing embraces to singing together, the singer made sure to express her gratitude for those who have been supporting her. In one heartfelt moment that evoked cheers from the packed crowd, Karol G made a hand heart with a teary-eyed young fan while snapping a selfie. The singer closed out the unforgettable show with some of her fan-favorite bangers, including “Coleccionando Heridas,” “Si Antes Te Hubiera Conocido,” and lastly, the Tiësto remix of “Provenza,” turning the tropical cave into a rave-like party, while also waving the national flag of Colombia. title: ‘DTF St. Louis’ Creator Steven Conrad Has No Plans to Make More Movies
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking Hayden Panettiere, Actress in ‘Heroes’ and ‘Nashville,’ Dies at 36 close By David Canfield Plus Icon David Canfield Senior Entertainment Writer View All August 16, 2026 12:00pm Jason Bateman (left) and David Harbour in the HBO Max limited series. Courtesy of HBO When he was 19 years old, Steven Conrad sold his first screenplay, for Wrestling Ernest Hemingway . In the nearly 40 years since, the Florida native has gone on to write Oscar-nominated films ( The Pursuit of Happyness ) and create acclaimed TV series ( Patriot ), but he’s found a kind of career landmark with DTF St. Louis , his savvy exploration of middle-aged friendship and sexuality among Floyd (David Harbour), his wife, Carol (Linda Cardellini), and his new friend Clark (Jason Bateman). “I don’t think I’d been nominated for anything before,” Conrad says. Now he’s up for Emmys for producing, writing and directing the HBO limited series — which received 13 nominations. “I haven’t made anything that had this kind of attachment to this thing in our business,” he says. “It’s all new, and I don’t know quite what it means. But I’m happy that people are watching the show. That means a lot to me.” Related Stories TV 'The Pitt' Showrunner Admits Season One's Notoriety Amped Up Pressure For Season Two: "We Had to Prove That It Wasn't Just a Fluke" TV 'The Beast in Me' Showrunner Knows That the Violent Murder Scene Was a "Potential Tune-Out Point" For Some Viewers Conrad talks with THR about exploring male friendships, directing his own writing and why he’s focusing on television for now. There’s a lot of admiration for the way that you explored modern male friendship in this show. Can you talk about the approach you took and the conversations it’s sparked? It’s the sort of thing that can go missing from your life — a meaningful friendship, one that you can invest some of your emotional life in, to get good news and then want to share it with this person. When you’re a kid, maybe it just happens a little more regularly, but when you grow up, it can really vanish without you even knowing that it did. There can be periods where you just have a realization that you just don’t have all that many people that you would consider friends. Most of us have colleagues and family members, extended family members. When you are able to absorb the entire run of DTF , it’s positioned initially as this MacGuffin, with this murder case. What it really amounts to between the characters, Clark and Floyd, is some means to organize their friendship around some naughty thing that they can talk about in the fort privately. It had more to do with stimulating their friendship than stimulating their sexual lives. And then I guess it latched on to a period where men were starting to realize in real life that these friendships were not there. There’s also a unique exploration of sexuality among the three of them. What were you hoping to find there? Carol’s sexuality is very different from Clark’s, which is very different from Floyd’s. If you have these things, these appetites like Clark has — to want to do X, Y, Z with an intimate partner, and he hasn’t explored those with his partner — they don’t go away. He doesn’t have the courage to incorporate this into his marriage, so what is your obligation to those kinks? Clark allowed me to write about that type of individual sexuality, the person who has forestalled an exploration of the depths of their sexuality. I don’t think I would’ve felt good about a show if I only had one character who was swimming in those waters because they’re all so different. I felt confident when there was more than one, and that this could be a set of deliverable themes. It became important to me to try to do it in a way that seemed genuine and relatable to anybody who is living and breathing and has grown up. As you mentioned, you open the show with this crime frame that is more familiar to a TV viewer, but it gets more complex and original the deeper you get. What were some core moments for you in understanding that balance? The launching points I have for a story deepening are different from other writers — for me, they’re images. Wanting to install a swing set in your backyard, which is all Clark wanted to do; it’s heavy and he needed his friend to help, but there’s a moment where he just found himself blocked and seated on a swing next to this new friend. When that landed for me, I knew I was going to block that scene that way, then the childish need to be with another person sometimes just to feel safe or to cope. You would think you’d get meaning and then blocking — that you wouldn’t get blocking and then meaning. Being able to direct my own writing, which eluded me for most of my career, now I can explore knowing that I’m going to control the directing part of writing for film. It’s allowed me to discover stuff like that. And then casting is not something anybody really cares to ask a writer’s opinion about generally, but they have to contend with my opinion now. And casting two guys who I just knew that they would be giving off this magnetism and they could draw each other together. You work primarily in TV now, after previously being associated with movies. What’s the appeal of the longer format? If you’re good at making serialized TV, one of the things you then will be good at is delivering episodes and then delivering seasons and then delivering a series. There are three different ways to occupy an audience. There have to be three different approaches to this story. I took that so seriously that in the TV show Patriot — the first one that this crew all made together — when it came time to present the episode titles, we ended up using handcrafted one-off art each time. I treat episodes very differently. They have their own arc; their own payoffs; their own beginnings, middles and endings. Caring to try to be good at doing that at the end of the day leaves you feeling proud about the feat. It’s a lot of work. I haven’t obligated myself to a film or been connected to a film for a few years now, and I don’t have any plans to do it. It just seems it’s kind of gone from my future, this idea that I would make films again. My appetite to continue to make television is really it now because of the length of the engagement. It’s also a longer engagement with the audience. People think about that differently than they do their favorite movie. Films just feel like they’re in frames in a museum to me. Like The Godfather — I admire it. But I feel connected to Succession . I know they’re not my family, but there’s an attachment I have to the extended ordeal that everybody has gone through and the multiple characters that makes me feel like I’m not outside it. That’s what television means to me today. Do you think that the week-to-week release also helps that? This was one show where I observed it gaining this momentum to become appointment Sunday-night viewing. There is something in the ritual of the night. We got lucky that we were on Sunday night because that’s an important night at HBO. Somehow the universe just quiets down over the course of Sunday afternoon into a hush. You’re feeling all this dread — everybody knows the Sunday feelings about school on Monday — so people were in that frame of mind. I like it if a show comes out every Sunday night. I don’t know if I would like it so much if it was Tuesday at 7 p.m. This story first appeared in an August stand-alone issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine. To receive the magazine,

title: In ‘A Vineyard for A Lobster,’ Snowfall in a Ugandan Village Becomes a Political and Colonial Allegory
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking Hayden Panettiere, Actress in ‘Heroes’ and ‘Nashville,’ Dies at 36 close By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 16, 2026 11:45am 'A Vineyard for A Lobster' Courtesy of Locarno Open Doors Snowfall in Uganda? Welcome to the world of A Vineyard for A Lobster , one of the works-in-progress film projects presented during the 2026 edition of Open Doors , the Locarno Film Festival ‘s co-production platform and talent development program for filmmakers from equity-seeking communities and regions where artistic expression is at risk. It is in the works from Talemwa Pius (short films Engaito , Rations , Bitingu ) and producer Emmanuel Gashumba of Uganda’s Gripmagic Uganda Limited. The team behind the project, presented during the second edition of Open Doors with a focus on films from Africa, was one of the two main winners of the Open Doors Grant. Related Stories Movies "It Was a Bumpy Ride!": Jack Rowan and Director Kieron J. Walsh on the Many Lives of Head-Bopping, Troubles-Set 'Skintown' Locarno Open Doors Spotlight 2026 'Too Much Music' Is a Doc Project About Ghanaian Keyboardist Kiki Gyan - and About Who Controls Artists' Narratives THR has compiled highlights about the movie and insight from Pius about the project and the themes it explores. Synopsis The equatorial village of Rukumba has endured months of drought when suddenly snow falls overnight, an impossible event blanketing the land in white. Kamuturaki (48), a failed trader once mocked for selling winter jackets under the blazing sun, becomes an overnight success. Byeitaka (40), a disgraced preacher, declares the snow divine and sells melted snowflakes as holy water to frightened followers. Kagoro (38), the timid chairman, watches his authority erode as the village reorganizes itself around the miracle. When British envoys arrive, promising support for Rukumba’s independence from Uganda in exchange for access to the snow for scientific research, the village committee embraces the deal as progress. As competing ambitions take hold across the village, tensions rise and unrest erupts, forcing Ugandan military forces to intervene. By the time the snowfall melts, Rukumba is no longer a community but a collection of competing interests each convinced the miracle belongs to them. Director’s note A Vineyard for a Lobster grows out of my interest in how colonial structures continue to shape authority, belief and communal life in Uganda decades after independence. It begins from a question of what happens when something foreign enters a fragile social order and exposes what was already unstable. In the film, an impossible snowfall in a Ugandan village becomes a political allegory, echoing colonial intrusion. Its origin is never explained; what matters is what it reveals. As each character assigns the snow’s meaning according to their needs, the village begins to fracture. I explore how collective failure forms through ordinary self-serving decisions. The arrival of outside interests reflects a pattern that has shaped much of Uganda’s history, where promises of advancement often come tied to the erosion of local agency. I want the film to feel grounded and unsettling, immersing the audience in a community breaking under its own contradictions. What was the inspiration for you to want to make this film? The film came from a question that has been sitting with me for a while. What really changed after colonialism, and what didn’t. Growing up in Uganda, you get used to certain things just being the way they are. But at some point you start feeling that a lot of these colonial systems are still there. The way authority works, even how belief is organized. It looks stable on the surface, but there’s always tension underneath it. The idea of snow falling in a drought-stricken village came as something like a foreign presence entering a place and forcing people to respond to it in different ways. From there, the story became about what that kind of presence would expose in the village. The snow doesn’t break the village. It brings to the surface what was already unstable, so we can finally see it clearly. Almost like putting a face and name to it. And then the question becomes, now what. How do we become responsible to each other? How do we build better systems? I’m interested in how people react to it. Some try to profit from it. Some turn it into belief. Others try to control it. And in the middle of all that, you start to see how weak the sense of collective responsibility really is. That’s where the film comes from for me. Not the event itself, but what it reveals about people when something bigger than them enters their world. How universal are the themes of the film, and why should people outside your home see it? Even though the film is set in a small Ugandan village, it’s really about colonialism across time. Not just what happened in the past, but what carried forward, and what is still happening now in different forms. You can see it in how resources are controlled and how decisions are made for communities from the outside. The film speaks to people who have lived through that kind of history, and also to those who are experiencing it in the present, whether they call it that or not. Because at its core, it’s about what happens when something external or foreign enters a system and begins to reshape it, and how people respond to that kind of pressure. At the same time, it’s also about responsibility. About what happens inside a community when systems are weak, when accountability is not strong, and when people start choosing individual survival over collective responsibility. We are very conscious of that while developing the film. Even though it has a strong commercial direction, we’re also thinking about how it can create impact beyond the screen. We’re already considering an impact campaign that can engage with communities where these questions are still very present, not just in Uganda but in many parts of the world. So the film is not only meant to be watched but it’s meant to start these kinds of conversations. What is the next step for you and your collaborators after Open Doors? Right now the focus is on writing the script. Open Doors helped clarify a lot of things, so the next step is to sit with that and push the project into a solid draft. At the same time, we’re continuing conversations with collaborators we connected with in Locarno, and looking at how to structure the project for the next stage of development and financing. We’re also considering a short film version of the project as a way to further explore the world and tone, and to build momentum around it as part of the larger journey of the feature. So the focus is really just on moving the project forward in a concrete way, both on the page and around it. THR

The ex- Disney CEO and Thrive Capital boss Josh Kushner have scored the Los Angeles Lakers at a valuation of $12.5 billion, Deadline has confirmed. That’s the highest valuation for a sports team in U.S. history, topping the record set when current owner owner Mark Walter bought the team just over one year ago. They will be buying out Walter’s 80% stake in the team. The deal came together in three days.” Angel City FC stakeholder Iger and Kushner, the once-FIFA-touted financial player (and Donald Trump family member by marriage), take a controlling interest in the one-time home of Magic, Shaq and Kobe from Mark Walter about a year after the Guggenheim Partners CEO bought the Lakers from the Buss family at a valuation of $10 billion . While Walter got close to 80% of the franchise, the the Buss family trust retained a 15% interest. According to The Athletic , Kushner owns a minority stake in the Miami Heat, which he will likely have to divest. League rules specify that no one can own interest in more than one team. Given the soaring cost of franchises, NBA owners in 2024 voted to allow private equity groups to buy minority stakes in multiple teams, but not a controlling interest. Kushner also once owned a minority strake in the Memphis Grizzlies. He started Thrive Capital in 2009 with backing from Peter Thiel, according to The Athletic. Iger came on as a minority investor in 2022. Earlier this year, Thrive Capital launched a holding company called Thrive Eternal, whose investments, said Kushner, would be in “iconic franchises and cultural institutions rooted in tradition, identity, and shared experience.” The holding company is, according to The Athletic , the vehicle by which Kushner and Iger intend to buy the Lakers. Thrive Eternal was one of the investors in the controversial recent plan by FIFA president Gianni Infantino to create a $20 billion commercial arm of soccer’s world governing body by selling stakes in the World Cup and other events. That plan was scuttled after widespread outcry in the soccer world and beyond.
